title: Free lord, dutiful servant
hookLine: Luther's Freedom of a Christian: free through faith, servant through love
tomorrow: what goes first on a list of things you got wrong?

cards: Volunteer hours get logged for the application. Favors get tracked in a quiet mental ledger: I helped you move, so you owe me a ride.
Martin Luther opens a short book, The Freedom of a Christian, with two sentences that tear up the ledger. A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none.
A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. Nobody's servant, and everybody's. He means both.

teach.h: FREE FROM ALL, SERVANT UNTO ALL.
teach.b: The question: why serve anyone, if nobody can make you?

teach.h: FREE BY FAITH, SERVANT BY LOVE.
teach.b: Luther finds his riddle in Paul: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all." Free how? By faith, Luther says.
A person is made right with God by trusting God's promise, not by a pile of good works, and nothing outside can take that away. Servant how? Through love.
Someone with nothing left to earn can turn every work outward, toward the neighbor who needs it. His boldest picture: be a kind of Christ to your neighbor.
Churches put faith and works into words differently: Lutherans follow Luther's way of saying it, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of faith and good works together, in their own terms.
A neighbor tradition knows this servant too.

In the Mishnah, in the sayings called Pirkei Avot, Antigonus of Socho teaches: don't be like servants who serve the master for the sake of a reward; be like servants who serve with no reward in view, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.
Shared ground: service that isn't payment.
One honest difference: Luther's servant serves because faith in Christ has already set him free, and the service runs toward the neighbor.
Antigonus speaks of serving the Master, God, directly, with the fear of Heaven upon you.
Two traditions, each in its own words, and a servant who isn't keeping score.

how: Lutherans read The Freedom of a Christian as a short summary of Luther's teaching on faith and love; Christians of other churches read it too, and speak of faith and works in their own terms.

s: for Luther, freedom means owing nobody anything
the popular sense. his free person has nothing to earn, and so is free to serve everyone.
Luther takes his riddle of freedom and service from Paul

games.q: you tutor a younger kid every week. his family can't pay, and he never says thanks. a friend asks, 'why bother? you get nothing.' what's Luther's answer?
o: fair point; service should at least be noticed.
nothing to earn is exactly what makes it free service.
keep going, because it earns your place with God.
games.why: for Luther, faith has already set the Christian free, so every work can turn toward the neighbor, and it's free because it isn't payment.

practice: Bring to mind one person who can't pay you back, or won't even notice: a tired neighbor, someone eating alone, someone in a care home. Write a short message offering one plain help, and use the sit to decide when to send it.
If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Free lord. Luther's name for a Christian set free by faith, who then, through love, becomes servant of all.

orig.note: Latin, from Luther's Latin text: a most free lord.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: free, and servant, with nothing owed in either direction. See you tomorrow.
